title: AI first pass of the disclosure checklist, with cited answers
problem: Disclosure checklists run to hundreds of questions that reviewers answer by hand against the client's statements, typically taking several hours per engagement, and missed disclosures can become inspection findings.
approach: The tool reads the draft statements, works through each requirement, proposes a cited answer with rationale, and flags questions it cannot support.
The auditor accepts, edits or rejects each suggestion; Caseware says only approved answers are written to the engagement file.
Caseware beta firms saved 2.7 hours per checklist run on average (vendor-published); Thomson Reuters reports about 30% uptake among eligible customers (vendor-published).

title: Disclosure-checklist and statement analysis built into Big Four audit platforms
problem: Auditors must complete required disclosure checklists, evaluate compliance with disclosure requirements and review draft statements before sign-off.
approach: KPMG announced in April 2025 a Financial Report Analyzer in KPMG Clara whose output helps auditors complete disclosure checklists.
Deloitte announced in June 2026 Omnia agents that include evaluating disclosure compliance; PwC said it plans statement review and tie-out tools.
Auditors complete the checklists and make the decisions; preliminary conclusions go to professionals to review. No outcomes published (self-reported).

title: AI second look at a completed checklist, flagging answers that differ
problem: Long checklists cause reviewer fatigue and firms roll last year's checklist forward; Caseware's beta found completed checklists with answers that were wrong because a requirement was misread.
approach: The tool runs against the auditor's own answers and flags where its reading of a requirement differs, so effort goes to disagreements.
Caseware reports beta firms also used its agent as a quality check on checklists already completed.
In one beta case it surfaced questions answered incorrectly through misinterpretation (vendor-published); the auditor resolves each flagged divergence.

title: AI proposes 'No' and 'Not applicable' answers on disclosure requirements
problem: Conditional requirements such as 'if material' need professional judgment, so they lean on experienced staff and limit how much juniors can do.
approach: Thomson Reuters says future Disclosure Review will extend to harder calls like 'No' and 'Not applicable'; no release date given.
Ideagen's tool already marks items it cannot find as No for the user to review.
Human checkpoint for the future feature is not specified; today a senior or manager decides applicability and materiality. No outcomes published (vendor-published).

title: AI review of management reports against statutory disclosure rules (German Big 4)
problem: Auditing the management report has relied on a manual, checklist-based approach; reading front-section text for inconsistencies with the statements is tedious, and late edits break cross-references.
approach: A task-specific AI system at a German Big 4 firm links report passages to statutory requirements, checks calculations and highlights version changes.
Auditors review and document suggestions passage by passage, with dual-control review; the tool does not replace professional judgement.
Surveyed auditors judged it improved effectiveness and efficiency, more for standard tasks than complex ones; perception, not a measured error rate (independent).

title: Automated checking and tie-out of draft financial statements, re-checking only changes
problem: HLB Mann Judd Perth reviews over 300 sets of financial statements a year, about 1,200 hours on first-draft reviews alone; its earlier Excel add-in crashed and lost review marks.
approach: Caseware Validate runs thousands of checks in seconds and carries earlier checks forward, so later drafts need only the changes re-checked.
HLB Mann Judd Perth reports about 600 hours saved a year; MHA's trial cut casting from 25 to 12 minutes (vendor-published).
Managers and seniors review the output, focusing on key risks and disclosure completeness; preparers or reviewers clear each exception before issue.
who: HLB Mann Judd Perth, MHA, Caseware, Suralink

title: Agents draft financial statements and keep re-validating them (Fieldguide Field Financials)
problem: Fieldguide says preparing financial statements has needed a fragmented mix of reports and spreadsheets.
approach: Fieldguide announced three agents: one drafts a rolled-forward first draft from the prior-year report and current trial balance data.
A second validates continuously and flags stale overrides when adjustments change; a third rolls forward footnote language and fills schedule-driven disclosures.
Practitioners stay in the reviewer's seat, per Fieldguide's CEO; how review is recorded is not described. No outcomes published (vendor-published).

title: Engagement-file review assistant tracking open issues and sign-off readiness
problem: Manual file review re-performs work by hand, and PCAOB staff found inspected firms with at least one engagement quality review deficiency rose from 37% in 2020 to 42% in 2022.
approach: Caseware announced cross-file risk checks, unresolved-issue tracking and review pack generation for managers, and earlier sign-off visibility for partners (vendor-published).
In a Caseware scenario a reviewer asks if the team missed anything; the tool surfaces a variance against board minutes.
Fieldguide lists a reviewer agent rolling out later in 2026. The reviewer decides what holds and what goes back.

title: Tool analyses audit committee communications to surface issues earlier (PwC)
problem: IFIAR's 2025 survey found audit committee communications findings in 79 of 725 inspected audits, against 24 of 593 in 2024; PwC wants such issues handled sooner in audit preparation.
approach: In October 2026 PwC's US assurance leader said another tool analyses audit committee communications for 2026 year-end audits to surface issues sooner.
The source does not say which communications the tool reads or who uses its output; no human checkpoint is described.
No outcomes published (self-reported).

title: Predictive or language model gives auditors a going-concern signal (BDO Netherlands)
problem: Going-concern assessment is a matter of significant judgment, and traditional machine-learning bankruptcy models struggle with complex, unstructured data.
approach: In Spain an audit firm used a decision tree as a supplemental guide and compared its suggestions with the auditors' reports.
In the Netherlands a language model combined financial data with audit-report text to predict bankruptcy within two years, shown to BDO accountants.
On 20 case studies, accuracy was model 85%, control group 77%, LLM-assisted group 78%, with no speed difference (independent).
The accountant makes the going-concern call; the prediction and summary are inputs.
who: BDO Netherlands, a Spanish audit firm

title: Idea: tools stress-test management's going-concern assessment and its data
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: the revised going-concern standard strengthens the auditor's evaluation of management's assessment and takes effect for periods beginning on or after 15 December 2026.
approach: The standard's application material says automated tools may help with sensitivity analysis, such as discount or growth rates, on management's assessment.
They may also help evaluate the reliability of large volumes of data from several sources used by management.
The auditor evaluates management's method, assumptions and data. No outcomes published (independent).

title: Idea: AI proposes key audit matters for comparison with the team's
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: auditors choose key audit matters from significant matters discussed with governance, a professional judgment, and views differ on how useful disclosures are.
approach: A 2026 University of Genoa thesis tested a language model identifying key audit matters from the annual report alone, then compared them.
A 2024 seminar abstract reports AI predicted approximately 37% of auditor-reported critical audit matters (independent).
The auditor decides which matters qualify; the thesis concludes AI can support the process without replacing professional judgement.

title: Generative AI drafts audit memos and documentation for professional review
problem: AI-drafted audit text can be fluent and wrong; Big4News reports EY Canada withdrew a research report with 16 of 27 references hallucinated, though not an audit document.
approach: PCAOB staff reported in July 2024 that some firms let staff use generative AI for initial drafts of audit memos and presentations.
Deloitte's June 2026 announcement lists drafting documentation and developing preliminary conclusions among its Omnia agent examples.
Professionals review the agents' conclusions; the team member stays responsible. A named person checking each cited source is only an idea.
who: Deloitte, firms named by PCAOB staff

title: ChatGPT used across audit preparation, fieldwork and reporting in internal audit (Uniper)
problem: Internal audit teams draft engagement reports and related documents as part of every audit.
approach: Uniper's internal audit function uses ChatGPT in audit preparation, fieldwork and audit reporting tasks.
The function estimates efficiency gains of 50 to 80 percent from initial tests across various processes, including reporting (self-reported estimate).
The authors also report the key risks, challenges, and rules Uniper adopted. Human checkpoints are not described in the abstract.

title: Idea: a language model reviews financial statements for errors against accounting standards
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: researchers say manual financial statement auditing is inefficient and error-prone, and auditors still miss errors despite extensive verification.
approach: One benchmark maps errors to violated standards; models found errors given transaction data but were weak at citing standards and completing audits.
A separate unsupervised method flags likely misinformation using past statements and audit reports, demonstrated on 11,460 financial statements over 5 years (independent).
The auditor explores flagged data sources and business processes to validate suggestions.

title: Idea: a language model checks XBRL tagging and cross-document consistency
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: tagging errors in filed statements, such as sign flips and unneeded custom tags, still draw SEC comments; auditors do not attest the tagging.
approach: The FinAuditing benchmark of 1,102 real-filing instances tests whether language models can match concepts, extract taxonomy relations and reason across documents.
Thirteen models showed substantial gaps in concept retrieval, relation modelling and consistent cross-document reasoning (independent).
A named reviewer owns the tagging review.

title: Idea: a reviewing agent checks the preparing agent's work before humans sign
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: as agents prepare more of the file, human review becomes the bottleneck and the main control.
approach: The AICPA practice aid says one AI tool may help the auditor evaluate another, without reducing supervision and review duties.
The UK Financial Reporting Council guidance says reviews may be done by humans, other language models or rules-based protocols.
The human reviewer and partner still sign. No outcomes published (independent).

title: Idea: an agent completes and reviews staff-level workpapers across the engagement file
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: preparing workpapers consumes staff time before review, and limited access to proprietary audit data has constrained measuring where agents can be relied on.
approach: FinancialAuditBench sets 90 workpaper completion and review tasks across six synthetic engagements and evaluates eleven frontier models.
Agents completed substantial portions of staff-level tasks well but sometimes performed inappropriate procedures or produced incorrect documentation (independent).
Caseware has a Document Intelligence Agent in closed beta. Professional review remains necessary where agents are not reliable.
